newsitem.title: UK: Global bull market returns below par - study.
newsitem.headline: Global bull market returns below par - study.

text.p: The seven-year bull market in world equities is the longest since World War Two but is still below average in real return terms, according to a study by Templeton Investment Management.
"This is now the longest bull market in the post-war period," said Sandy Nairn, Templeton's director of global equity research.
The current rally in global equity markets has produced an inflation-adjusted return of 86.6 percent since October 1990, versus an average of 103.1 percent in bull runs since 1954.
But even so the rally is looking pretty ripe to Nairn.
"I would not stop investing in equities but if I had a lump sum I would give serious consideration to averaging my investments over a period of time," he said.
Templeton reconstructed the MSCI World Index back to 1954 in order to examine equity boom and bust patterns.

He cautions that even though returns in the current bull market are not unprecedented, the averages are somewhat skewed by the phenomenal 1982-1987 rally, ended by the Black Monday crash after producing five-year returns of 302 percent.
That rally, bolstered by the fall of communism and the ascent of Thatcherism and Reagonomics, cannot be expected to repeat, according to Nairn.
"We are going to have a bear market sometime. I can't tell you when but in the average one you will see equity holdings fall by about 25 percent over a 12 month period," Nairn said.
And Templeton is now finding the stock picking pretty thin.
"It is more difficult to find value," Nairn said.

Cash holdings in the $1 billion in funds Nairn managers has risen in recent months to about 20 percent, partly because money keeps pouring in from investors but substantially because acceptable buys are difficult to find, he said.
"We want to get it invested but it is a hard job."
Nairn has been scaling back his U.S. holdings but sees value in the UK manufacturing sector.
Hard hit by the precipitous rise in sterling, UK manufacturers have fallen out of favour with investors to the extent that valuations have become attractive, he said.
"We started finding large numbers of undervalued companies so our biggest net investment in recent months has been in (UK manufacturers)," he said.
But in general Nairn is feeling cautious.
"Sometimes valuations are so cheap you would say get your money in right now.
"This is not one of those times."
One finding of the study is that volatility in world equities as a whole has actually reduced in recent years, despite spectacular swings in individual markets.
Nairn pegs this to the rise in value of equity markets outside the U.S. and Japan
"More diversity means less volatility," Nairn said.

The overall lesson to be learned from the bull and bear study, he says, "is that if you want to be invested in equities you want a widely diversified portfolio and you want to have a five-year time horizon."
"Within most five year time spans you have a bear market where values drop by about 25 percent. If you are forced to sell at the end of that it is pretty ugly."
